results.summary: This project implements a custom 8-bit RISC-V-inspired CPU with a hardware multiplier, 32 bytes of RAM, and custom branching instructions. It uses a multi-cycle finite state machine for fetch, decode, and execute, and includes a bootloader mode for loading programs via the input pins. The CPU is controlled by external signals for reset, mode selection, and clock, and outputs the destination register value and program counter for monitoring. It is notable for its high-density synthesis on the IHP26a process and its use of a 1x2 tile area.

This project is a 4-bit Johnson counter (ring counter) that produces a pattern where only one output pin changes per clock cycle. It is implemented with standard cells and is intended for educational demonstration of sequential logic. The counter is clocked externally and its four output pins display the internal state. It is notable for its simple, observable shifting pattern.

This project is described as a simple ALU with embedded registers, but the documentation is inconsistent, mentioning a 4-bit counter and 7-segment display. It likely performs arithmetic or logic operations on register values and may output results to a display. The design is intended for educational purposes, demonstrating basic ALU and register functionality. The exact behavior is unclear due to incomplete documentation.

This project is a digital synthesizer that generates audio waveforms and outputs them via a DAC. It uses an SPI interface for control and can produce various tones or waveforms. The design is intended for music generation and is notable for its waveform generation capabilities. It is implemented in digital logic and requires external audio hardware.

This project is a simple Verilog design that shifts a VGA image on the screen. It outputs a VGA video signal and likely uses a framebuffer or image data. The design is intended for graphics display and demonstrates image shifting. It requires a VGA monitor and possibly external memory for the image.

This project is a factory test structure that includes a timer, SPI interface, and ring oscillator. It is designed for testing chip functionality and performance. The SPI interface allows external control, and the ring oscillator provides a clock source. It is notable for its use in chip validation.

This project implements a scan chain for testing and debug, with a granularity of 4 steps per bit. It is controlled by a microcontroller or CPU via an SPI interface. The design uses standard cells to minimize area and is notable for its low-power operation. It integrates test and debug features into the chip.

This project is a VGA display design that requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and optionally an SPI controller and external SPI ROM. It is experimental and uses a 6x2 tile area. The documentation is incomplete, with testing details still to be confirmed. It is notable for its experimental nature and potential for graphics display.
